label: 31 Aug 2026
summary: ROCm speculative serving made the largest step: full HIP-graph capture for Kimi-K3 plus DSpark raises measured output throughput 3.83× at concurrency 1 and 1.88× at concurrency 16, with a 1.60 GiB-per-rank capture-memory cost.

Blackwell kernel work is splitting into prepared, shape-specialized paths: FlashInfer reports a 3.18× geomean for a prepared BGMV MoE pipeline and about 5× for grouped MXFP8 quantization in controlled kernel-only tests.

Correctness remains performance engineering: SGLang eliminates GPT-OSS BF16 all-reduce non-finites at a measured 0.3% cost, while vLLM caps speculative graph sizes after an earlier expansion caused H200 startup-memory failures.

Two llama.cpp changes show small dispatch details can dominate locally: native AMD permutations add 33–35% Q2 decode throughput on an RX 9070 XT, and a fast MoE token-grouping path adds 9.9% prefill on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.
No qualifying new arXiv or OpenReview paper appeared in the strict weekend window; this edition therefore focuses on merged, benchmarked framework changes.

items.title: vLLM: Full HIP graphs for AITER MLA speculative decoding
items.one_sentence_takeaway: Moving AITER MLA verification metadata work outside capture lets Kimi-K3 plus DSpark use full HIP graphs, raising reported output throughput from 12.10 to 46.30 tok/s at concurrency 1 and from 174.01 to 326.46 tok/s at concurrency 16 on 8×MI355X.
items.problem: ROCm speculative decoding could not reach full graph capture: one draft attention group advertised an overly weak support level, and the AITER MLA verify path performed four device-to-host synchronizations plus dynamic allocation inside the captured region.
items.why_it_matters: Speculative decode repeatedly executes small verification steps where launch and synchronization overhead can dominate; falling back to piecewise capture leaves much of the latency benefit unrealized.
items.existing_approaches: PIECEWISE graphs captured only graph-safe segments. The metadata builder also bounded a verify buffer from max_model_len when the worker lacked the real KV capacity.
items.limitations: Full capture raises graph memory from 0.51 to 2.11 GiB per rank. The published random-token workload had only about 21% draft acceptance, so its absolute token rates are not representative of real prompts.
items.proposed_solution: Advertise UNIFORM_BATCH for non-causal multi-token draft groups, expand verify metadata once per step outside capture into persistent buffers, and propagate the actual KV-cache token capacity to size the reservation.
items.key_differences: The patch removes capture-breaking synchronization instead of merely wrapping more operators, while keeping the remaining data-dependent sync in the external metadata builder.
items.results_with_conditions: 8×AMD MI355X, TP8, Kimi-K3 target, DSpark draft, seven speculative tokens, 1,024-token input / 256-token output, random prompts. PIECEWISE→FULL: concurrency 1 output 12.10→46.30 tok/s and ITL 186.98→34.26 ms; concurrency 16 output 174.01→326.46 tok/s and ITL 188.28→92.91 ms. Capture memory 0.51→2.11 GiB/rank; acceptance length remained about 2.5. The verify-buffer reservation fell 295.3→46.6 MiB/rank after using real cache capacity.
items.assessment: The day’s strongest end-to-end result and worth deep reading for ROCm speculative stacks. The performance/capacity trade-off is real, and production traffic with higher acceptance should be re-benchmarked before extrapolating.

items.title: FlashInfer: Prepared Blackwell BGMV MoE backend
items.one_sentence_takeaway: An opt-in SM100 prepared backend combines pointer-stable workspaces, deterministic reductions, and one CUDA Graph launch, delivering a reported 3.18× geomean kernel-pipeline speedup across 14 BGMV MoE shapes on GB200.
items.problem: The existing BGMV MoE shrink/expand path pays repeated launch, setup, and output-initialization costs, which are disproportionately expensive for small token batches and LoRA-routed expert work.
items.why_it_matters: Low-batch decode and adapter-heavy MoE serving frequently execute small routed matrix-vector workloads where microsecond-scale fixed overhead directly affects TPOT.
items.existing_approaches: The portable high-level BGMV path supports broad shapes but does not prepare one pointer-stable, graph-replayable pipeline specialized for Blackwell.
items.limitations: The generated backend is opt-in, SM100-only, and supports hidden sizes 2,688 and 3,072. Results are kernel-pipeline measurements, not model-level throughput or latency.
items.proposed_solution: Generate BF16/FP16 SM100 programs, preallocate stable workspaces through prepare_bgmv_moe, capture output initialization plus shrink and expand as one graph launch, and assign each output token one deterministic reduction owner.
items.key_differences: It fails closed for unsupported shapes instead of silently selecting a generated profile and avoids atomics by reducing routed pairs in fixed input order.
items.results_with_conditions: NVIDIA GB200, BF16, rank 32, 128 experts, top-k 2, eight LoRA adapters, one slice, hidden sizes 2,688/3,072, 1–1,024 tokens. Cold-L2 CUPTI span includes output initialization + shrink + expand. Existing path 47.6–307.7 µs versus prepared 12.9–116.3 µs; speedups 2.55–4.15×, geometric mean 3.18×. All 14 shapes passed correctness; 49/49 GPU/JIT tests passed.
items.assessment: High-value kernel engineering for a narrow but important Blackwell MoE/LoRA regime. Worth reproducing if the serving model matches the generated profiles; end-to-end gains remain unreported.

items.title: FlashInfer: Cake grouped MXFP8 quantization on Blackwell
items.one_sentence_takeaway: A deterministic Cake backend for grouped MXFP8 quantization reports 4.88× on B200 and 5.10× on B300 versus FlashInfer’s cuTile persistent kernel for one controlled B=2, M=256, K=4096 case.
items.problem: Grouped MoE inputs need per-group MXFP8 quantization before low-precision GEMMs, and the existing general cuTile path leaves substantial fixed and scheduling overhead in this tested shape.
items.why_it_matters: Quantization sits directly on the routed-expert critical path; its latency can erase the compute savings of low-precision MoE GEMMs, especially at modest token counts.
items.existing_approaches: The default cuTile backend is portable and persistent but slower in the reported Blackwell shape. Generic dispatch can also blur whether unsupported generated profiles fell back silently.
items.limitations: Only one B/M/K shape is published, and timing isolates one quantization kernel with allocation and Python work excluded. No downstream grouped-GEMM or end-to-end serving result is reported.
items.proposed_solution: JIT-compile exact SM100/SM103 CUDA profiles, keep output allocation and prepared schedule outside the timed region, preserve ragged masks and 64-bit offsets, and expose Cake as an explicit opt-in backend.
items.key_differences: The backend produces byte-exact E4M3/UE8M0 outputs and fails closed when no matching architecture/shape profile exists.
items.results_with_conditions: B=2, M=256, K=4096, BF16 input, preallocated outputs, strict cold-L2 CUPTI kernel-only timing. B200: 18.880→3.872 µs (4.876×); B300: 18.943→3.712 µs (5.103×); cross-architecture geomean 4.988×. Each GPU passed 33 targeted tests plus CUDA 13.3 memcheck/synccheck with zero errors.
items.assessment: A convincing microkernel result with unusually careful measurement hygiene. Worth reproducing for matching MoE shapes, but the single-shape evidence is not enough to infer an end-to-end speedup.

items.title: SGLang: Prevent BF16 overflow corruption in ROCm QuickReduce
items.one_sentence_takeaway: Power-of-two range scaling removes more than 106 million non-finite elements from a GPT-OSS-120B TP4 QuickReduce workload while adding only 0.3% to the measured 90 MiB collective latency.
items.problem: QuickReduce converts BF16 activations to FP16 before reduction; GPT-OSS activations above FP16’s 65,504 ceiling became infinity and contaminated entire 32-value codec blocks.
items.why_it_matters: A fast collective that silently corrupts activations invalidates model output. The failing 90 MiB collective came from the shipped auto-derived chunked-prefill configuration, not an artificial edge case.
items.existing_approaches: Native BF16 reduction was numerically exact but 17.6% slower at 90 MiB. The existing FP16 path had no conversion-range guard; quantized codecs already normalized blocks but could still clamp finite accumulator overflow.
items.limitations: The fix guarantees finite outputs and exactness for the FP codec in tested cases, but quantized codecs may still clamp finite sums above the FP16 accumulator range. Validation is limited to MI350X/MI355X and captured workloads.
items.proposed_solution: Scale CodecFP inputs by the exact power-of-two S=16 in FP32 before narrowing, undo the scale on output, explicitly emit packed FP16 conversion, and enable the hardware FP16 overflow-clamp mode on gfx942/gfx950.
items.key_differences: The compile-time exponent shift is graph-safe and preserves the fast FP16 transport path; it avoids runtime range detection and leaves already normalized Q4/Q6/Q8 codecs at S=1.
items.results_with_conditions: GPT-OSS-120B, TP4, four MI350X/MI355X GPUs, ROCm 7.2, 16,384-token chunked prefill, 90 MiB collectives: non-finite outputs fell from 106,493,184 of 574,757,475,840 reduced elements to zero. Median collective latency over 400 iterations was 590.3→592.1 µs (+0.3%); native BF16 was 695.8 µs and RCCL 852.4 µs. Error versus FP32 was unchanged to ten significant figures in captured tests.
items.assessment: A production-critical correctness fix with excellent forensic evidence and negligible measured cost. Strongly worth reading and backporting for ROCm GPT-OSS deployments using QuickReduce.

items.title: llama.cpp: Native AMD permutation for Q2_0 dot products
items.one_sentence_takeaway: Replacing a generic HIP byte permutation with native AMD instructions raises reported Q2_0 token generation by 33–35% on an RX 9070 XT while preserving roughly 1,000 tok/s prompt processing.
items.problem: HIP’s generic byte-permutation sequence for Q2_0 dot products used LDS and excess registers on gfx1201, constraining the quantized decode kernel.
items.why_it_matters: For low-bit local inference, the vector dot-product path is exercised across most model layers, so an inefficient bit-unpacking primitive directly limits token generation.
items.existing_approaches: The portable fallback used a generic permutation sequence with 47 VGPRs and 16 KiB fixed LDS. It was correct but poorly matched to modern AMD hardware.
items.limitations: End-to-end numbers come from one RX 9070 XT, one Q2_0 workload family, and ROCm 7.2. Other architectures were compile-checked, not performance-benchmarked.
items.proposed_solution: Use the AMD permutation builtin that lowers to eight v_perm_b32 instructions on supported gfx targets, retaining the fallback where the builtin is unavailable.
items.key_differences: The new path removes LDS traffic and reduces VGPR use from 47 to 39 while exhaustively validating all 65,536 packed Q2 values.
items.results_with_conditions: AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT (gfx1201), ROCm 7.2 / clang 21. Token generation: tg128 42.06→56.78 tok/s (+35.0%), tg256 41.93→56.74 (+35.3%), tg512 41.81→55.64 (+33.1%); prompt processing remained about 1,000 tok/s. All 65,536 packed permutations matched and 12,727 ROCm backend tests passed.
items.assessment: A strong, concrete low-level optimization for RDNA4 quantized inference. Worth reproducing on the exact model and quantization type; portability of the instruction is better supported than portability of the speedup.

items.title: llama.cpp: Fast CUDA token grouping for ten-expert MoE routing
items.one_sentence_takeaway: Generalizing llama.cpp’s warp-lane grouping to ten selected experts removes a kernel that consumed 13.3% of prefill time and improves reproduced Qwen3.8-Flash-Next prefill by 9.9% at 55K context on an RTX PRO 6000.
items.problem: The fast mm_ids_helper path only accepted expert counts dividing 32 plus a hard-coded six-expert case, so ten-expert routing fell back to a serial per-token loop with a warp reduction.
items.why_it_matters: Token-to-expert grouping precedes every MoE matrix multiply; on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next it exceeded FlashAttention in the profile and consumed 13.3% of prompt-processing time.
items.existing_approaches: The generic path walks one token per iteration for every expert block. Existing optimized cases used fixed lane groups for 2/4/6/8/16/32 selected experts.
items.limitations: The merged dispatch adds the ten-expert case; other unsupported counts still need explicit cases. Decode is unchanged because a one-token batch has no grouping parallelism.
items.proposed_solution: Round the selected-expert count to the next power of two for lane grouping, rely on the existing padded-lane guard, and dispatch n_expert_used=10 through the optimized helper.
items.key_differences: The fast path’s real constraint is lanes per token, not whether the expert count divides the warp; the patch generalizes the existing six-to-eight padding logic.
items.results_with_conditions: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000, CUDA, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with 512 experts / top-10 routing, 55K-token context, warm alternating builds: prompt processing 2,139→2,351 tok/s (+9.9%). Generation was unchanged. A separate compile/pad-guard probe on RTX 3080 Ti verified two groups per warp with all padded lanes safely skipped but did not reproduce end-to-end performance.
items.assessment: A focused and credible prefill optimization for top-10 MoE models. Worth backporting if profiling shows mm_ids_helper overhead; it does not benefit already optimized expert counts or single-token decode.

items.title: vLLM: Dual-stream MoE decode inside ROCm graphs
items.one_sentence_takeaway: Launching the shared expert before dispatch enables HIP-graph-compatible overlap with routed experts, yielding workload-dependent TPOT gains on 8×MI300 while automatically disabling unsafe or regressive configurations.
items.problem: Simply enabling the existing multi-stream mode on ROCm launched the shared expert only after routed experts completed, creating sequential execution; unquantized shared inputs could also alias routed inputs and race.
items.why_it_matters: Shared and routed experts are independent work in many MoE decoders. Overlap can reduce TPOT without changing model math, but race conditions or communication interference can silently damage accuracy or regress throughput.
items.existing_approaches: Sequential execution is safe but leaves parallelism unused. Fused shared experts can be faster but are unavailable with some all-to-all backends such as MoRI; naïve dual-stream execution regressed TP and raced on unquantized Qwen3.5 inputs.
items.limitations: Enabled only for ROCm data parallelism with quantized routed-expert input. It is disabled for TP and mixed/prefill batches; several tested concurrency points regressed, and fused shared experts remained faster where supported.
items.proposed_solution: Launch the shared expert on an auxiliary stream before expert dispatch, make the ordering graph-compatible, and gate the feature on DP plus non-aliased quantized inputs.
items.key_differences: The feature includes automatic safety/performance gating rather than exposing a blanket multi-stream switch.
items.results_with_conditions: 8×AMD MI300, DeepSeek-V3-0324, DP8/TP1, random 1K/1K and 8K/1K input/output, concurrency sweeps. At 1K/1K c64, TPOT 45.66→43.51 ms (+4.71% improvement); at 8K/1K c32, 68.29→60.48 ms (+11.44%). Regressions appeared at 1K c16 (-6.77%) and 8K c16/c128 (-3.07%/-3.71%). GSM8K showed no material accuracy change; Qwen3.5’s unsafe unquantized path is disabled.
items.assessment: Useful, carefully gated overlap work rather than a universal win. Worth reading for ROCm MoE schedulers, but operators should sweep their own concurrency and prefer fused shared experts where compatible.

items.title: SGLang: Dense per-layer KV views for unified MHA/SWA memory
items.one_sentence_takeaway: SGLang replaces strided page-envelope slices with dense per-layer MHA/SWA KV views, preserving measured serving speed while establishing the layout needed for FA3, FlashInfer, TensorRT-LLM MHA, and FlashMLA backends to consume the unified pool.
items.problem: Unified MHA/SWA memory exposed strided per-layer slices inside a page-major envelope; only the Triton backend reconstructed the required four-dimensional view.
items.why_it_matters: A memory-pool design tied to one attention backend prevents operators from combining unified KV allocation with the best kernel for a model, GPU, and request shape.
items.existing_approaches: Triton translated the strided envelope internally, while MLA already used dense per-layer views. Other attention backends could not safely read MHA/SWA unified memory.
items.limitations: This PR lands the layout prerequisite, not the downstream non-Triton readers. Models with asymmetric K/V row widths are rejected at startup, and no direct speedup is expected.
items.proposed_solution: Expose dense K/V tensors per layer with one shared block table, derive tail padding from sub-pool specifications, and switch IDs, sizing, and pool entry points atomically.
items.key_differences: The change standardizes MHA/SWA on the dense layout already used by MLA and explicitly fails unsupported asymmetric head dimensions instead of failing later during pool construction.
items.results_with_conditions: Production configuration with radix cache, overlap scheduler, CUDA graphs, and page size 256 where possible. Heavy-decode: 512-token prompts / concurrency 128; radix-retract: 4K shared-prefix prompts / concurrency 192. Across Qwen3.5-9B, Kimi-Linear-48B, Falcon-H1-7B, and GPT-OSS-20B, median ITL deltas ranged from -1.01% to +1.22%. Sixty unified-versus-baseline accuracy pairs produced 68/68 clean cells.
items.assessment: Architecturally important enablement with good non-regression coverage, but not yet a user-visible backend expansion by itself. Worth reading if modifying SGLang’s unified KV allocator or landing the follow-up backend readers.

items.title: vLLM: Cap speculative CUDA-graph sizes after H200 memory regressions
items.one_sentence_takeaway: vLLM now keeps auto-generated speculative decode graphs below the platform’s existing default ceiling after wider captures caused H200 startup OOMs and cut available KV cache to 0.94 GiB when 5.12 GiB was required.
items.problem: The earlier widest-batch capture change appended speculative decode sizes beyond established defaults—2,176 and 6,400 tokens in two H200 jobs—causing full-graph OOM or starving the KV cache.
items.why_it_matters: Graph coverage is useless if capture memory prevents the server from starting or removes the cache capacity required by the workload; default policy must balance launch savings against persistent memory.
items.existing_approaches: The previous patch captured every widest uniform speculative batch by default. A proposed full revert would restore memory safety but discard useful dynamic sizing and safe off-stride coverage.
items.limitations: Shapes above the default ceiling now execute eagerly unless users explicitly opt into larger capture sizes. The primary source reports CI failure reproduction and configuration tests, not a completed model-throughput comparison.
items.proposed_solution: Cap generated uniform-decode sizes at the platform default—512 tokens on H200 and 1,024 on data-center Blackwell—while retaining exact off-stride full graphs that fit under the ceiling.
items.key_differences: This is a narrow corrective follow-up to PR #50488, preserving its safe sizing logic rather than reverting all 621 lines.
items.results_with_conditions: H200 nightly configurations: DFlash produced a 2,176-token capture width and suffix decoding 6,400; one job left only 0.94 GiB KV cache versus 5.12 GiB required. The patch pins both regression widths and passed 26 targeted configuration tests (one skipped). Model evaluation and end-to-end latency/throughput were not reported in the primary source.
items.assessment: Operationally important and a useful correction to yesterday’s graph-coverage story: capture policy needs a memory budget, not just shape coverage. Worth backporting if using speculative defaults; users choosing explicit larger graphs must capacity-test them.
